messages.text:
We propose replacing blanket confidentiality and approval with the following terms for the three-depot trial.

1. **Internal use.** Each party may use trial measurements for operation, maintenance, safety assessment and evaluation of the trial. Access to raw failure traces and firmware parameters is limited to named trial-team members who need them for those tasks and are bound by confidentiality. An external maintenance contractor does not gain access solely by servicing a depot.
2. **External reports.** A party planning to release a trial report externally will give the other party the proposed text and 10 working days to review it. The reviewer may identify restricted material for removal and flag factual errors for correction. After the review period, the author may release the report once it has removed restricted material and addressed factual comments. Silence does not extend the deadline. Disclosure of raw failure traces or firmware parameters requires express written agreement, subject to the safety exception below.
3. **Aggregate uptime.** Sensor maker may publish a single uptime figure pooled across all three depots, with the reporting period and calculation method. The publication will omit route and depot identifiers and breakdowns that could identify either. The same review period applies, and separate publication approval is unnecessary.
4. **Urgent safety disclosures.** Either party may immediately give the minimum information needed to a recipient able to act on an urgent safety risk. The disclosing party will notify the other as soon as practicable afterward, identifying what it shared, with whom and why.

For the maintenance workflow, what decision must the contractor make, and could it make that decision from a fault code, affected-unit ID and recommended action? If a specific repair requires trace analysis, we propose that a named trial-team engineer examine the trace and return diagnostic findings. If that would leave the contractor unable to complete the repair, please identify the task and the data it requires so we can agree on narrowly scoped access.

We propose adopting your text with the following changes.

1. **Maintenance.** The contractor needs to decide what to repair or replace and whether the unit can return to service. A fault code, affected-unit ID, recommended action and post-repair test criteria are enough when they identify a clear repair. The operator may give those details to the assigned technician under written confidentiality. If the test fails or the fault recurs, a named trial engineer will examine the trace and send diagnostic findings. If the technician still needs a trace excerpt or firmware parameter to complete a specific test, the operator’s maintenance lead and the maker’s trial engineer may jointly authorize that disclosure in writing for that repair. The technician will receive only the necessary fields, use them only for the repair and delete them when the ticket closes.

2. **Monthly board reporting.** The operator may give the transit board a monthly summary of pooled uptime, failure counts and repair outcomes across all three depots, including in a public board packet. The project leads will agree on a template and calculation method before the first reporting month. The operator’s trial lead will check each report against the template and authorize release without further maker review. Reports will omit unit, route and depot identifiers, exact event times and depot/time pairs. If a rare event could still identify an employee, the operator will combine categories, use a longer reporting period for that measure or suppress the figure. The same safeguards apply to the maker’s pooled uptime publication.

3. **Safety and compulsory disclosures.** The operator’s safety lead may report a serious incident promptly to the competent authority, including after the immediate danger has passed. Either party may also disclose information needed to address an urgent safety risk or meet a mandatory reporting obligation. These disclosures require no prior clearance and may include traces, parameters, locations or timestamps to the extent needed by the recipient. The disclosing party will notify the other afterward as soon as practicable and legally permitted, stating what it shared, with whom and why. Notice must never delay the report or response.

4. **Other publications.** For the maker’s pooled uptime publication and other external trial reports outside the agreed board template, we accept your 10-working-day review. The reviewer will identify the specific passage at issue and the confidentiality concern or factual correction. The author’s project lead makes the release decision after the review period, removes identifying details, corrects verified errors and omits disputed restricted material unless both leads clear it in writing. Silence ends review on schedule. Publishing raw traces or firmware parameters always requires express written agreement from both leads.

We accept the monthly board reporting, safety and compulsory disclosure, and publication terms as drafted. The operator’s trial lead may release a monthly board report that follows the agreed template. Reports outside that template, including our pooled uptime publication, follow the 10-working-day review.

We agree that routine repairs and return-to-service checks can proceed without raw data. We propose one change to the maintenance clause so the team can handle an exceptional repair while keeping restricted data within the trial team. Please replace the final two sentences of clause 1 with the following text.

> If the diagnostic findings are insufficient for a specific test, the operator’s maintenance lead and the maker’s trial engineer may jointly designate the assigned technician in writing as a trial-team member for that ticket only. The authorization must identify the technician, the test and the minimum trace fields or firmware parameter needed. Before receiving access, the technician must be bound in writing to use those data only for the authorized test and to limit sharing to named trial-team members working on the ticket. When the ticket closes, the technician’s designation and access end, and the technician must delete any retained copies.

With that substitution, we accept the full text.
We accept the proposed substitution. It replaces the final two sentences of clause 1. With that change, both parties agree to the full text for the three-depot trial.

We propose adding three disclosure tiers. At a single-vehicle depot, even an uptime percentage can identify the vehicle’s operator. The board can still receive evidence of exceptional failures if we separate the public figures from the evidence used for oversight.

1. **Public board packet and maker publications.** Publish uptime only as a pooled three-depot figure. Before release, the publishing lead must check whether the figure or an accompanying failure count could identify an individual when combined with earlier reports or public schedules. If so, combine categories, extend the reporting period or suppress the affected figure. The agreed board template and the maker’s 10-working-day publication review continue to apply.
2. **Confidential board oversight.** For each exceptional failure, the operator may give designated board reviewers bound by confidentiality a case summary under a non-identifying case number. It may describe the failure, its operational impact, the corrective action and the return-to-service test result, including any unresolved issue. A named trial engineer will verify the summary against the underlying record. The leads will agree on the case-summary template in advance so the operator can use it without case-by-case clearance. If board procedures require a summary to be made public, only the public-tier version may be used, subject to the agreed compulsory-disclosure clause.
3. **Trial-team evidence.** Raw traces, firmware parameters and the link between a case number and its source record stay with the authorized trial team, subject to the agreed safety and compulsory-disclosure exceptions. A board reviewer may request a specific follow-up check by case number. The engineer will record what was checked, the result and any limits on the conclusion, and provide that finding through the confidential tier.

We propose treating a failure as exceptional if it triggers a safety report, recurs after repair or leaves a unit unable to pass its return-to-service test. Would those triggers and an engineer-verified case summary meet the board’s evidence requirement? If the board requires independent verification, which finding must an independent reviewer verify, and can the board receive that finding confidentially?

We accept the three exceptional-failure triggers and the pooled public uptime figure. An engineer-verified summary meets the board’s routine evidence need. For an exceptional failure, the confidential subcommittee also needs to inspect the suppressed result itself. We propose the following additions.

1. **Public release.** The operator’s trial lead may release the monthly packet on the board schedule after checking for identification against public schedules and earlier releases. Both publishing leads must also check for identification by subtraction. For example, a pooled figure and two depot totals can reveal the remaining depot’s result. The maker’s publications retain the 10-working-day review.

2. **Confidential inspection.** The operator’s safety or maintenance lead will log the case number, date and basis for inspection when any one of these occurs: the incident triggers a safety report, the same fault recurs after a completed repair, or the unit fails its return-to-service test. Within one working day of logging the trigger, the operator’s trial lead may give designated confidential subcommittee members read-only access to the affected suppressed measure, its calculation basis and the case summary. A named trial engineer will mark which findings have been verified and which remain open. Pending verification must not delay access to the available result. The subcommittee may request a documented recheck by case number. That allows it to examine the basis for the finding without routine access to employee identities, exact depot/time pairs or raw traces. We do not require a separate independent reviewer.

3. **Rapid contractor access.** When a unit is held out of service after an incident and the assigned technician needs a trace to isolate the fault or validate the repair, waiting for an engineer’s diagnostic summary can delay the test. We propose that the maintenance lead and maker’s trial engineer jointly approve in advance a roster of named technicians, specific tests and the minimum trace fields for each test. For a matching incident, the on-duty maintenance lead records the ticket, technician, test and reason the routine diagnostic details are insufficient. That entry activates the technician’s ticket-only designation. The operator will provide secure access to the approved excerpt within 30 minutes of activation and notify the maker’s on-duty engineer at the same time. Tests or fields outside the written authorization still require joint ticket-specific approval. The agreed confidentiality, access expiry and deletion terms apply.

Can your on-duty team support the preapproved trace access within 30 minutes? The safety lead’s authority to notify authorities promptly applies independently of both the repair and board timelines.

We accept the public-release checks, including the check for identification by subtraction. We also accept read-only inspection by designated confidential subcommittee members within one working day of logging an agreed trigger. Members may inspect the actual suppressed measure, its calculation basis and the case summary, including findings marked as open. The calculation basis may show the inputs needed to check the arithmetic. Employee identities, exact depot/time pairs, raw traces and firmware parameters remain outside the inspection materials. Any onward public release follows the public-tier rules.

We can support the 30-minute arrangement **if the operator can grant access without waiting for a maker engineer to respond**. We propose the following activation language.

> Before a roster entry goes live, the maintenance lead and the maker’s trial engineer must jointly approve the named technician, test and minimum trace fields in writing, confirm the technician’s written confidentiality obligations and test the operator’s ability to grant secure access within 30 minutes. For a matching incident that leaves a unit out of service, the on-duty maintenance lead activates the technician’s ticket-only trial-team designation by logging the ticket, technician, test and reason routine diagnostics are insufficient. Within 30 minutes of activation, the operator grants access to the approved excerpt and simultaneously notifies the maker’s on-duty engineer. Maker acknowledgment is unnecessary. Access ends at ticket closure, when the technician must delete any retained copies. An unlisted test, additional trace field or firmware parameter requires joint written approval for that ticket.

The safety lead may notify the competent authority promptly, independently of either timeline. Can the operator provision the approved excerpt on each covered shift under this arrangement?

Yes, for each shift that passes the access test. Before we mark a shift as covered, its on-duty maintenance lead must demonstrate that they can grant the named technician secure access to the approved excerpt within 30 minutes using that shift’s credentials and without a maker response. We’ll record coverage with the roster entry. Until a shift passes, the existing joint ticket-specific approval process applies on that shift.

We accept your activation language and the confidential inspection terms. On a covered shift, logging a qualifying activation starts the 30-minute clock. The operator grants access and notifies the maker’s on-duty engineer simultaneously. The safety lead may report to the competent authority immediately, independently of the access and board reporting timelines.

We accept the shift-specific coverage condition. The operator will record coverage on the roster only after the on-duty maintenance lead demonstrates, using that shift’s credentials, that they can grant the named technician access to the approved excerpt within 30 minutes without a maker response. On a covered shift, logging a qualifying activation starts the clock. On other shifts, joint written approval for the ticket remains required.

This completes the tiered disclosure addendum. The safety lead retains authority to report immediately to the competent authority.
